description:
Brindaban Matri Mandir is the oldest Barowari Durga Puja in Kolkata, established in 1910 at Sukia Street, North Kolkata. For more than a century, the puja has remained connected with the religious, social and cultural life of the neighbourhood.

Theme- Shoye Santosh
SANTOSH DUTTA | 2 December 1925 – 5 March 1988

A shining star of the Bengali world of acting, Santosh Dutta was far more than a character actor. He became an enduring part of the Bengali imagination—of its humour, mystery and emotions. Even today, Santosh Dutta remains a cherished “Parash Pathar” (Philosopher’s Stone) in the hearts of Bengalis.

Born on 2 December 1925 in undivided Bengal, Santosh Dutta came to our locality at the age of just seven, accompanying his father to their home at 49 Amherst Row. He lived in that house, “Suradhwani Kutir,” for the rest of his life.

It was Satyajit Ray who brought Santosh Dutta from the theatre stage to the world of cinema. Although he became widely known as a comedian, the range of his acting was remarkably diverse. In every character he portrayed, one could discover an effortless, unmistakably Bengali quality.

From the “Researcher” in Hirak Rajar Deshe, to Abalakanta in Ogo Bodhu Sundari, and, of course, Jatayu—Lalmohan Ganguly—the beloved character from the Feluda series.

Through this centenary presentation, we are therefore setting out to celebrate the beloved spirit of Bengali identity and culture through the memory and work of Santosh Dutta.

The artist’s vision will bring memories of Santosh Dutta to life through different characters, scenes, light and shadow, and installations. Visitors will embark on a nostalgic journey where the lanes of old Kolkata, the atmosphere of cinema sets, the ambience of the theatre stage, and cherished moments from Bengali life will come alive once again.

Each scene will become a frame of memory.

Each light will evoke the brilliance of his acting.

Each character will bring back days filled with laughter, wonder and affection.

Through the harmonious combination of sculpture, lighting, ambience and art, this presentation will become a heartfelt tribute from Bengalis to Santosh Dutta—a celebration of the centenary of a legend.

“Once again, upon the screen of memory, it will come alive…”

KALODHWANI
For generations, the Bengali Panjika (almanac) has remained deeply woven into Bengali life, rituals and festivities. From dates, tithis and auspicious occasions to social information, curious advertisements, old typography and illustrations, the Panjika is also a fascinating document of its time.
Naktala Udayan Sangha’s Durga Puja 2026 explores the origin and evolution of the Bengali Panjika—its many forms, what its pages contain and omit, and why it continues to remain relevant even today.
Through old pages, printed letters, illustrations, advertisements and distinctive printing styles, the theme revisits a familiar yet gradually fading world of Bengali time, belief and everyday life.
